speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the committee will recall that when this vote was under consideration last week the question of the retirement of Dr. Torrance was discussed. Some of the files I had not with me at the time, and I think it was the request of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) that when this matter was again before the committee I should bring the balance of my files. I have done so. Inasmuch as the letter written by Dr. Mohler of Washington has already been read to the committee by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I do not purpose to place it on Hansard again unless requested so to do.
The Mohler letter that we asked for was another letter.
In reply to a letter from Dr. Torrance.
No, another letter that the minister said he had, casting certain reflections upon Dr. Torrance. I read the official letter from Dr. Mohler.
There is only one that I know of.
The hon. minister intimated there was another letter from Dr. Mohler reflecting upon the action of Dr. Torrance.
No, there is just the one communication, which my hon. friend placed on Hansard.

I distinctly remember the minister suggesting that Dr. Mohler had reflected upon Dr. Torrance. I should like to

Supply-Agriculture
know what he based that suggestion on if there is no further letter from Dr. Mohler.

If the hon. member will wait-he asked me for my files-he shall have everything in consecutive order. The next letter I have that I think will be of interest deals with the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). He took the ground that he did not think Dr. Torrance had been quite fairly dealt with in the matter of his annuity, in that he had been led to believe that he would get $1,500 based upon seventeen or eighteen years' service, whereas he was allowed only $900 based on eleven years' service. I think it is quite obvious that we could not make any such arrangement inasmuch as the amount of annuity is governed by statute, and I believe I can show that I made this quite plain to Dr. Torrance in my correspondence. Here is my letter in reply to Dr. Torrance, which I think clearly indicates the nature of his letter to me, and therefore in order to expedite matters I will not read his letter unless the committee so request. I have all the orders in council that were passed in connection with this matter, but I do not want to clutter up Hansard with all these documents. On August 29, 1923, I wrote to Dr. Torrance as follows:
Dear Doctor,-
On my return to the city this morning I find your favour of the 22nd instant awaiting my attention. Replying, I note what you say with respect to the decision of those having authority in such matters, that your retiring annuity under the terms of the Calder Act would be approximately $900 instead of $1,500 as anticipated.
When you decided to retire under the terms of the Calder Act you and I could not possibly come to any agreement as to the definite amount of the annuity, as that was, as I understood it, determined by the act itself which I had not then consulted.
What I did agree to was that I would recommend to my colleagues that, in addition to any annuity you might be entitled to, you would also receive six months' leave of absence (including the legal two months) with pay, and that I have done. This was subsequently authorized and is now being paid. But this recommendation was discretionary on my part, while the Calder Act, like most other legislation, was mandatory and therefore obviously beyond my power to change or depart from.
Regretting any misunderstanding you may have experienced respecting the amount of annuity connected with your retirement, I am,
Yours very truly.
Then later Dr. Grisdale had some correspondence with him. On January 8, Dr. Grisdale wrote to Dr. Torrance as follows:
Dear Dr. Torrance,-
I have your letter of the 5tli instant, in regard to your retirement, and as you will note if you read the order in council, a copy of which was sent to you- the minister did recommend that your period of service should be counted from 1906, and his report to council along these lines was signed and submitted, but representations were made to the Treasury Board by the Auditor General, and it was upon these representations that the period of service, and, consequently the amount of the annuity was reduced. I can assure you that as far as the minister, the department and the Civil Service Commission were concerned, all possible steps were taken to have your annuity based on the seventeen years service, but in view of the criticisms of the Ayditor General, the Treasury Board saw fit to modify the recommendation.
Yours very truly,
To that Dr. Torrance replied from Guelph on January 14, as follows:
Dear Dr. Grisdale,-
I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 8th inst. and am glad to know that both the minister and yourself did what you could to have my annuity based on seventeen years' service as I was led to expect.
I regret that your efforts and those of t he minister were unsuccessful.
Yours sincerely,
Now, that is the end of the correspondence.
Is there a letter in the file dated January 5?
Yes, from Dr. Torrance to Dr. Grisdale. Does my hon. friend wish me to read that?
Yes.

It is as follows:
Dear Dr. Grisdale,-
I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 2nd inst. enclosing cheque for a gratuity of two months' salary and a copy of the order in council respecting my retirement.
I regret that the government has not seen fit to carry out the terms of my retirement as stated to me by Hon. Mr. Motherwell as it appears to me to be a distinct breach of faith not to have done so. I was induced to retire on certain statements of his in regard to the matter and I had no doubt that they would be honourably carried out.
Yours sincerely,
I have already quoted the letter from Dr. Grisdale indicating to Dr. Torrance that my recommendation in the matter had corresponded with Dr. Torrance's expectations but that the Audit Board would not let it go through. Now what information had the Audit Board on which to base their decision? This is information, I may say, that I had not at the beginning, neither had I the Calder Act before me to make a computation, even had I known the number of years that Dr. Torrance claimed his retirement should have been based upon. Here is a letter written by Mr. Jarvis to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission, dated August 21, 1914, on the question of the length of time the Audit Board and the Auditor General thought should be counted as continuous service on the part of Dr. Torrance. The letter reads:
Supply-Agriculture

Dear Sir,-Replying to your letter of the 18th instant, re the retirement of Dr. F. Torrance, I have to advise you that Dr. Torrance was appointed a veterinary inspector under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, by order in council of March 1st, 1906, appointment to be effective from January 1st, of the same year.
From the Auditor-General's reports, it would appear that payment's made to Dr. Torrance during the period of 1906-12 were as follows:-
This was the period that was under dispute, the period which Dr. Torrance thought should count in working out his annuity. The rest of the letter indicates the length of time he was employed between 1906 and 1912, when he became Veterinary Director General and continued as such up to his retirement. The letter points out that in 1905-6 he received in payment of his services $339.29 as salary and expenses, period not available. In 1906-7 he received $150. In 1907-8 he was not employed, and in 1908-9 he was not employed. In 190910 he received $150 salary for ten days' work. I assume it is all based on a rate of $15 a day. so that it is easy to figure out the length of his employment on that basis. In 1906-7 at $15 a day he would have been employed ten days. There are three consecutive years in two of which he was not employed at all and in one of which he was employed for only ten days. .Then in 1910-11 he got $60 in salary, and that was apparently at a lower rate, for some reason, for it covered a period of six days. Then in 1911-12 his total salary and expenses amounted to $172.70, period not available. From August first, 1912, up to the time of his retirement was the period of continuous employment, and the Auditor General and the Audit Board took the ground that only that period could count, because during the previous years his service was of an intermittent nature. In view of the fact that in two of those previous years he had not been employed at all and in one of them for only ten days, I do not see how anybody could strain his generosity to the extent of calling that consecutive employment. That may be a matter of difference of opinion. But so far now as I understand justice and continuous employment I feel that the Auditor General was perfectly justified in taking the ground that the whole period could not be regarded as continuous employment.

Was the intermittent nature of the employment not due to the lack of disease at that particular time? Was he not that class of veterinary who worked under fees rather than on general salary, being engaged only when there was work for him but still being in the employ of the department all this time, his name appearing on the files at Ottawa as a regular inspector?

We have no information of that nature. Such information as we have just came to us incidentally; it is not on file. He was busily employed at the Agricultural College at Winnipeg, but we have no information that there was no disease prevalent and that that was the reason he was not employed. He was paid on a per diem basis; we have one or two on that basis yet, but not very many and that is in cases where the amount of work to be performed is so small as not to justify an annual engagement. The veterinary is just employed on a per diem basis as some outbreak occurs, whether it is glanders, T.B., or whatever it is, and I presume Dr. Torrance was employed the same way. Of course, a man on a per diem basis must be employed before he is warranted in getting the pay. If Dr. Torrance had got an annuity based on seventeen years' service, as I first recommended, I think I would have had far more difficulty in defending that than I would have in defending what he has got based on the estimate of the Audit Board and the Auditor General. I scarcely think, Mr. Chairman, that the point that the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) brings up would affect the case.

I asked the minister when he began to read his file what he based his statement upon that Dr. Mohler had condemned Dr. Torrance's action. That was the impression that he left with the committee, if he did not state it in so many words.

I would prefer not to be discussing Dr. Mohler. He is not a resident of Canada. We have his communication. I have already read one letter, and there is nothing to be gained by unnecessarily repeating it.

But the minister did not hesitate the other day to make that statement. He certainly left the impression with the committee-and I think the statement is here on Hansard-that Dr. Mohler had condemned Dr. Torrance's action, so I do not see why he should be so particular about it now.

My hon. friend
recalls the incident the other day. I had been asked by an hon. member, I forget whom at the moment, if I had any additional-reasons. The question was, why did I wait six or seven months before Dr. Torrance was retired? Well, I was busy, the session was approaching, in fact, the session was on during part of that period, and I was willing to let matters run on and see if Dr. Torrance would

Supply-Agriculture
get over his resentment, because I believe he was resentful over the fact that he was not sent overseas; in fact, I know he was; he told me so himself; I had a conversation with him. Then what were the supplementary reasons I had? Well, I had a memorandum here. It has nothing to do with the letter upon which I base my justification for asking for his retirement. The right hon. leader of the opposition was so vociferous in demanding that I should read the memorandum that I did read part of it, and then he was equally vociferous in condemning me because I did read from a memorandum that had no name to it, and that is where it stood. I think I have recited the incident correctly.

I do not wish to change the trend of the discussion, but I want to draw to the attention of the committee a rather peculiar situation. The committee on Agriculture has been called for 8.15 this evening, and the Minister of Agriculture has now his estimates before the House. A good many members of this group are members of that committee, and I have no doubt that some of us who are here intend to go to that meeting. It is rather peculiar that these two committees dealing with agriculture should conflict.
What is the suggestion?

I was not suggesting an3'-
thing. I think it is all right for the minister to go ahead with his estimates, but it is rather a peculiar situation that two committees should meet at the same time, dealing with agriculture.

I think this is the way it happened. The estimates of the Minister of Customs were supposed to be taken up first, then Agriculture, then Trade and Commerce. In the absence of the Minister of Customs, I naturally followed with my estimates. I must confess that I entirely forgot about the meeting of the Agricultural committee. My duty now as I see it, is to carry on.

I listened with a good deal of interest to the debate on Friday last concerning the dismissal of Dr. Torrance, the late Veterinary Director General. While I regret to criticise the action of the Minister of Agriculture, I think the whole House agreed that the dismissal was a very harsh one, that Dr. Torrance had not been given a reasonable chance. Time to resign was not afforded him. He was called into the minister's office and told that the minister was finished with his

services, and his resignation was demanded on the spot. He was threatened that if he did not put in his resignation at once he would be dismissed and have no opportunity to receive any retiring allowance. These are the exact facts as they have been given to me.
I claim that if his offence was serious enough to get rid of him in that way, he should not have been given the opportunity to put in his resignation at all, but should have been discharged forthwith. But having been asked for his resignation, in view of the prominent position which he held at the head of a very important branch of the Department of Agriculture, a position that he had filled with great success for a period of ten years, he should have been given an opportunity to resign in a proper way. Here was a civil servant sixty-four years old, with only one year more to go, and without being given time to thing over his resignation, kicked out in this disgraceful manner. He requested the minister to give him until the following Tuesday to consider his resignation before putting it in, but he was compelled to sign it on the spot, the minister passing him paper and ink with which to do the work. Now when we consider the spirit of the Civil Service Act, an act that, while perhaps not working perfectly, has certainly been the greatest protection that the Civil Service of this country has had, it is obvious that such drastic action is not in keeping with what was intended to be the spirit of that act when it was put on the statute books.
Dr. Torrance was a man of particularly high qualifications, a university graduate before he took up the veterinary profession, a man who had worked for the Health of Animals branch intermittently before he took up the position of Veterinary Director General, a man who at that time was very highly recommended and was selected from a field of a number of other applicants for the position, and was considered the very best man then in sight. I perhaps have had a rather better opportunity to judge him than many others, for the reason that I worked for him for a numr ber of years in the capacity of chief inspector of the Health of Animals branch for the province of British Columbia, Dr. Torrance being my chief during that period. Later on, when I became Minister of Agriculture, he still continued in the position of Veterinary Director General, and I think he has rendered very excellent service to this country. He certainly cannot be condemned on the score of inefficiency, because in Canada we have held for a long time the high record of maintaining the healthiest herds of live stock in the world, herds that are practically free from contagious
Supply-Agriculture

disease. This was the condition when he left the department. During the time of the cattle embargo inquiry in London in 1921 there was no stronger argument that we could offer to the commission to induce them to give a verdict in our favour than the fact that we were maintaining our herds in a way that no other country in the world was able to do.
Then, too, Dr. Torrance during his period of office has made history in the veterinary line in Canada. In the first place we had mange for twenty-five years in a district in southern Alberta and in southwestern Saskatchewan covering an area larger than Scotland. This whole area was under quarantine. You could not move a hoof out of that district without inspection. Dipping was carried on from time to time, and the whole thing was a great nuisance to the farmers and also a source of great expense. In 1919 the eradication of this disease was undertaken. Plans were carefully laid during the fall and winter months and in the summer of 1920 I think some 220,000 head of cattle were subjected to a lime and sulphur bath twice, a very big job indeed, and the work was so perfectly done that at the end of that year we were able to cancel the quarantine in that area for the first time in a quarter of a century, all this being done at the time Dr. Torrance was Veterinary Director General. I am not going to say that he did not receive excellent assistance from his very efficient staff during that period -he certainly did.
Just at this particular point I might refer to one of the charges against Dr. Torrance which was brought in a letter presented by the minister. It was not a charge on which the dismissal of Dr. Torrance was based but it was one of the charges mentioned-about his taking his golf sticks out to Calgary when he went out there to attend the cattlemen's meeting at that time. This is surely a joke. I do not see that there is anything in the regulations to prohibit an official from carrying his golf sticks with him as long as he attends to his business. Surely there was no harm in carrying golf sticks both ways, more particularly when the railway company does not charge anything extra for doing so. Dr. Torrance also handled very skilfully the outbreak of dourine in southern Alberta. This disease appeared among horses and threatened to become very serious indeed. During one year it cost this country about $46,000 in compensation alone. The work of eradicating it was undertaken during the period that Dr. Torrance was Veterinary Director General and, with the 
co-operation of his able assistants, it was entirely wiped out.
In the United States in 1914-15 there was a very serious outbreak of foot and mouth disease which manifested itself in some twenty-two states, a number of which are contiguous to Canada's southern border. Although this outbreak cost the Americans some $10,000,009 our veterinary service along that boundary line was so efficient that not one single case of foot and mouth disease appeared in Canada. I am only mentioning this to show that Dr. Torrance could not be blamed on the score of inefficiency. He maintained the cleanest herds in the world, showed himself to be a gentleman in every way and a man of ability. He could be sent anywhere and win appreciation. He was frequently invited to speak in the United States at large gatherings, 'and was well known all over this continent for his ability. Under those conditions I do not think his dismissal was fair. Here was a man holding a high and important position discharged as though he was a mere nobody. I do not care how lowly a man's position in the Civil Service may be he is at least entitled to fair play and decent treatment from his superior officers, and more particularly from his minister.
The minister says that Dr. Torrance was a little disappointed at not having been included in the commission which went over to Great Britain to fix the regulations with the British government for the entrance of store cattle into Great Britain. Why should he not be? Was he not one of the proper officers to have gone? It was quite right to have taken the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, a man of ability, a man whose ability is recognized all over this country; but when on earth did Duncan Marshall graduate as a veterinary surgeon? When it comes down to a matter of regulation every veterinary who has had experience in administering the regulations of the Health of Animals Branch must appreciate the difficulties that are continually arising in connection with those regulations. I -know when appearing before the Embargo Commission on several occasions cases came up and questions were raised which only a veterinary surgeon could intelligently answer; and in that particular connection I claim that Dr. Torrance should have been included in the body that went over to Great Britain at that time. Why should he not have been? Seeing that he was at the head of the Health of Animals branch in this country, and that he felt his responsibilities very keenly why should he not have been included immediately it was

Supply-Agriculture
suggested to lower the quarantine period on cattle entering this country from Great Britain.
I remember when the period of quarantine was discus ed in London in 1921, it was claimed by one of the commissioners that Canada should be ready to deal with Great Britain on a fifty-fifty basis in regard to the quarantine period. I pointed out in the strongest possible way that that would be unfair, for the reason that we had had no foot and mouth disease in Canadian herds since 1884. During that year two shipments of cattle arrived from Great Britain-one on a steamer called the Mississippi, and the other on the steamer Oxenholme. One arrived in the month of May and the other in the month of June. Foot and mouth disease was discovered in these two shipments, but they were stopped at Point Levis station in Quebec and dealt with there. Both of these shipments, I repeat came from Great Britain. I pointed out to the British commissioners on the occasion referred to that in Great Britain during that particular year they had had twenty-two outbreaks within the first six months of the year, showing that the conditions in Canada and in Great Britain were not equal on the point of disease; and that while it was necessary to have a quarantine for a period of thirty days against the British cattle owing to the danger of foot and mouth disease, there was not the need for the same long quarantine period on cattle going to Great Britain from this country.
Now, let me make this particular point very clear:	In the regulations that at present
prevail between Canada and the United States for the handling of cattle crossing the boundary north and south we have a very satisfactory arrangement. This arrangement has been based very largely on the regulation of Canada guarding the entrance of cattle from other countries. In the same way the United States has adopted a similar system as a precaution in the matter of cattle or other live stock coming from outside countries. The result is that in accepting each other's conditions we are able to make regulations that are mutually satisfactory to both countries. If the quarantine period on breeding cattle from Great Britain had been lowered in Canada to a period of less than thirty days, the Americans would have become interested immediately. Why? Because letting in those cattle on a shorter quarantine than had been in existence certainly would increase the danger of American herds being infected by the infection of Canadian herds through this particular source. For that reason Dr. Torrance had every cause to feel the gravest
154i
possible alarm at any suggestion along those lines, and it was only to be expected that he should bring this matter to the notice of the minister.
It has been stated that Dr. Torrance in his correspondence with Dr. Mohler, chief of the Bureau of Animal Industry at Washington, used the word "political." What if he did? Does the minister say himself that he has never been troubled with political interference since he took office, or any of his officials? Although I was Minister of Agriculture for a period of two years only I had that experience on several occasions, and I think it is the experience of almost everyone who holds the position of minister in this country.
Referring to the letter to Dr. Mohler, let me say that these two men occupy similar positions, one guarding the health of animals in the United States and the other guarding the health of animals in Canada. They were on ve y familiar terms. They met every year at the annual meeting of the American Veterinary Association held on either side of the boundary. They were on the closest of terms, and these familiar relations between these two officers have been of great benefit to this country on many occasions. In my own experience I have known shipments of mangy cattle, although carefully inspected before leaving Alberta, to develop the disease at South St. Paul and in Chicago. At the particular period I am speaking of now there was a great agitation springing up in the United States to keep out Canadian cattle. Hon. gentlemen will remember in 1919 we sent over something like 540.000 or 550.000 head of cattle, and in 1920 we sent over something like 365,000 head, with the result that the Americans were becoming somewhat alarmed at the Canadian competition, and whenever any mange would appear in any shipment, there was a hue and cry to keep out Canadian cattle. The good relations existing between the two officials were useful in getting over any difficulty which might arise. On every-occasion Dr. Mohler has acted in a fair way in dealing with his Canadian friend in cases of that kind, with the result that no further restrictions were placed on our cattle. In the discussion last Friday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is reported at page 2238 of Hansard as saying.
Let us get back to the document itself. I say with all respect that I have never seen an officer in any department, and certainly have never had anything to do with one, who would write a letter of that character, especially to a foreign government in whose files it would be kept. There is no question that all the members of the staff would know about it.

Supply-Agriculture
I would like to call special attention to that. He continued:
And as a matter of fact, word came back to us that they were astonished at Washington that we should keep in our employ a man who would write such a letter.
Make a note of that. Then the discussion continues as follows:
Mr. Meighen:	Who said that? Will the minister
tell us who is responsible for the statement that the officials in Washington had expressed astonishment at the fact that, as he puts it, we should have kept such a man in our employ?
Mr. Motherwell: It came through Dr. Mohler.
Mr. Meighen: Very well; but who said it?
Mr. Motherwell:	I understand it came from Dr.
Mohler.
Mr. Meighen:	Did Dr. Mohler say that he was
astonished ?
Mr. Motherwell: Yes.
It appears to be very clear that this statement was credited .to Dr. Mohler, chief of the Bureau of Animal Industry in the United States. I am rather surprised that the minister should make any such statement, particularly considering the friendly feeling in that country. We are doing a large trade in live stock with the United States, and it is necessary that we should be on the most friendly relations with them. I wrote Dr. Mohler quoting these portions of Hansard, and sent him a copy, so that he would have everything before him very clearly. My letter reads as follows:
Ottawa, May 17, 1924.
Dr. J. R. Mohler,
Chief of Bureau of Animal Industry,
Department of Agriculture,
Washington, D.C.
Dear Dr. Mohler,-I have had the pleasure of meeting you on one or two occasions in Chicago, being introduced by the late Dr. J. G. Rutherford. You will perhaps remember me too as Minister of Agriculture for Canada during the latter part of the late administration.
I am forwarding to you herewith Hansard containing report of the proceedings in the House of Commons yesterday afternoon, May 16th. You will note that a debate was on concerning the retirement of Dr. Fred. Torrance, late Veterinary Director General.
During the debate (on page 2238) Honourable Mr. Motherwell, Minister of Agriculture, made the following statement-"and as a matter of fact word came back to us that they were astonished at Washington that we should keep in our employ a man who would write such. ..." On being further questioned you will notice that Mr. Motherwell stated "it came through Dr. Mohler." The question was then put, "Did Dr. Mohler say that he was astonished?" perhaps I should have substantiated this part of my argument but I intend to do it before I sit down-there was absolutely no ground for his dismissal; secondly, the manner of his dismissal was unwarranted and unparalleled for its crudity and for its almost-I was going to say-brutality having in mind the age of the gentleman; and I contend-
What about 1919?

And I contend further
that inasmuch as this resignation was secured by a distinct verbal agreement with the minister-
No.

The minister told us
that the other day.
I deny that absolutely.

Well I will read the
resignation again given under an agreement which should be observed. I say further that the meritorious services of Dr. Torrance are of a character, just as this order in council drafted by the minister himself or by his department sets forth, that wholly warrants the payment of the gratuity. Now let me read the resignation again. The minister may deny the agreement but I have it here in his resignation that the minister receives and acknowledges in writing, there is no gainsaying that:
I desire to express my wish to resign and retire under the Calder Act, understanding that I would now be entitled to a retiring allowance of fourteen hundred dollars per annum.
The exact figures were not worked out until later. Now I turn from that to what the minister says to-night and to the memorandum. The minister takes refuge in a certain position. The Prime Minister was not in his seat the other day and I regret that very much because I think we would have had a different story by now had he been here. The other day the minister stood up in his place and read a certain letter and said "I have had this letter in my possession for some months" -I think it was six or seven or eight months. He said "I was satisfied to retire him under this letter but I was looking for corroborative evidence, and I think I have corroborative evidence in my hands." And he held up a memorandum with a gesture that savoured of the melodrama. He of course was fishing but we did not fall for his bait. AVe insisted that he should not bluff this House. The minister said "It, reflects on Dr. Torrance therefore I do not read it". What more mean, contemptible method of besmirching the character of a man than to hold something before the public and say "I have something here that reflects on his character but while he is at outs with me now I am so courteous and jealous of this man's reputation that I prefer to keep this secret, but I have it here". I say what more contemptible methotf of besmirching an innocent man's character than to do that. And what did we do? We said to the minister "You are not going to get away with a cowardly act of that kind. If there is anything wrong in the memorandum, if there is anything detrimental to the character of Dr. Torrance we want to hear it, and the world wants to hear it, in ju-.tification of his dismissal." And vrhat did we get? We got a memorandum and the minister says "I would not have revealed these petty things if it -had not been for the fact that my hon. friends opposite insisted upon it." Now let us review these things for a moment, let us look the situation over. The minister got a memorandum and denied knowing anything about it. He would not tell us who wrote it, he said he did not know who the writer was. In the memorandum it is stated that he used the frank of a deputy minister for his personal mail and the personal mail of his family. Every Monday morning he brought his mail to the office and handed it to the messenger to be franked, and the Postmaster General wrote to him asking him in regard to the matter. Now, we have from

Dr. Torrance an absolute denial of any conscious violation of any regulations regarding the franking act. Let me say to the minister that Dr. Torrance had as much right to frank a letter for his family as the minister has to frank a letter for his family. Has the minister never franked a letter for any member of his family?
No.
Never?
No.
Well, a Daniel has come to judgment.

My family pay
postage on their letters.

I am very glad to hear it, but I will venture to say looking around this House that there are not many members but will frank a letter for their wife, son, daughter, or sweetheart. I will say to the House I have franked some myself.
I think a minister is entitled to do it if he desires.
I do not think there is very much wrong with it.
No.

And I think the civil
servants of Canada very frequently frank their letters. I admit that perhaps it may be well once in a while to bring up and demand a strict enforcement of the regulations, but I venture to say there is not a member of the House who can tell me what the exact terms of the regulations are. I am sure I do not know and I think I keep well within bounds. I am not aware of having franked a letter within the last five years for any one other than myself but I am conscious at some time in my thirteen or fourteen years' service in this House of having violated the rule as it is interpreted now. Is there anything in that worthy ol' even reference? There certainly is not. A kindly courteous word from the minister to any officer would at once end everything of that kind.
The dismissal was not based on that.

I know it was not but it was trotted out as corroborative evidence. Then the memorandum goes on to say that Dr. Torrance went to Calgary and took his golf clubs with him. This iniquitous memorandum which the minister said he could not and would not vouch for-he did not know Who wrote it, his deputy would' not tell 
him, and he would not tell the House although we asked him to do so-says that Dr. Torrance went to Calgary on official business, spent about fifteen minutes there on official business, and for the rest of the time he was there played golf. Now, we have a statement from Dr. Torrance that he never played golf in Calgary then or at any other time. Yet the minister comes into the House-and this is what angers me-and reads this memorandum impugning the honour and the integrity of this civil servant without a scintilla of evidence to back it up. The minister did not even take the trouble to ascertain who wrote this memorandum. Just think of it, the minister besmirching in a most iniquitous and picayune manner the character of a man, and he never himself tried to find out whether there was a scintilla of truth in his charges.
Now let me turn to this famous letter we hear so much about. The letter that Dr. Torrance wrote to Dr. Mohler. I wonder if the Prime Minister will bear with me while I read this letter again. I read it the other day. The minister was confronted with irrefutable proof that he was absolutely wrong with regard to the charge made last Friday and he says to-night "I stand to-night on this letter and if I had the thing to do over again I would not wait five months, I would dismiss him c.n the spot." He reiterates that.
That is not the way I put it. I said' I would take the advice of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie).
Oh, no. I ask the Prime Minister, he heard the statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what he said.
He said it twice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the way he put it.
I said that I would take the advice of the hon. member for Victoria and dismiss him immediately.
I heard that perfectly, but does the minister think the members of this House are children, that they cannot see through such absurd subtlety as that?
I|t is pretty hard to believe my hon. friend is sincere.
It is not hard to believe me at all.

To clear up that little question about the hon. member for Victoria dismissing Dr. Torrance without giving him a fair chance; I said that he should have had a fair

chance. I said that if his offence was serious enough to force his resignation, his resignation should not have been asked for, but he should have been dismissed outright. But when the minister saw fit to ask for his resignation he should at least have treated Dr. Torrance as a gentleman and as a man should be treated.

Dr. Torrance wrote a letter to the Acting Director General of the United States, and* I ask the House to look at it in the proper perspective. Canada was negotiating for the lifting of the embargo in Great Britain. The British authorities were suggesting to the Canadian authorities, "Now, if we admit your cattle into Great Britain we think you should lower the period of quarantine in Canada against British cattle which you import in some numbers, thoroughbreds and breeding stock". But there is a third party to this. Our regulations are more or less harmonious with those of the United States. Both the department in the United States and the department in Canada have been working in harmony; and so the minister directed Dr. Torrance-I think I am correct in this-to ascertain from the Director General of the United States what their attitude should be if the department found itself forced to lower the period of quarantine, and I have here the letter which the minister says warrants the dismissal of Dr. Torrance. I,t was marked "confidential" and was sent to Dr. Mohler of Washington. The letter reads as follows:
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge of the diseases against which we desire protection, of the conditions surrounding the traffic in animals, the freedom from disease of the country from which the cattle are exported, and the time occupied in ocean travel. If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine it places the scientific advisers of the respective governments in a very anomalous position, and I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
Let us pause there. This is the gist of the whole thing. This is where the minister takes his stand on the subject. Dr. Torrance says he had no idea of suggesting party or political influence of any sinister character. He was referring to the political pressure of the British government upon the Canadian government. Now were there not some grounds for that? Ample grounds. The British government were being asked to remove the embargo. We know that for years every conceivable opposition was put in the way. We know that the British farmers, agriculturists and breeders objected to it arid
fought it right down the line, and Canadian shippers were very much disappointed. But a time came when the British government felt that they had to do something. It was due to Canada to do it. There was some justice in Canada's claim, and they said to Canada, "Give us something which will be some compensation at least to our own people;" and they asked us to lower our quarantine regulations. That is the political consideration referred to, and I ask the Prime Minister in all fairness, would not the fair reading of this indicate that as a most sensible interpretation? Let me ask further, having in mind all this correspondence between the two departments of these two governments, and having in mind the question of the British embargo, the other end of the matter, what political considerations of a local or partisan character could possibly enter into it? There is no room for the suggestion. But as a matter of fact there were sound grounds for the political interference of the character I spoke of. He says in this letter:
It is quite possible, however, that a suggestion may be made that we should modify our quarantine so as to reduce the time of detention, and it is with regard to this possible demand that I would like to have confidentially your opinion as it affects the relations between the bureau and the Health of Animals branch. We have always felt that we were under agreement not to alter our quarantine regulations without previously notifying you of our intention, and we have received from you the same consideration.
Then he says:
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge.
I have read that portion. There is nothing wrong with that. Is that not perfectly sound? I have not the letter in consecutive form. I am just reading the paragraphs quoted in Hansard. He says in this letter:
I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
There is nothing wrong about that. Who should plan the regulations, if it were not to be done by the scientists employed by the different governments? Who is qualified to properly perform the regulations other than the Director General whose qualifications from that standpoint have never been questioned, not even by the minister? Let me pause for a moment to say that Dr. Torrance was dealing with this question as he was instructed to do by his minister. The only possible excuse the minister has for taking a political view of it is the word "political" inserted in that letter. If we can put on that word an interpretation consistent with the letter itself

as I have done-and I submit it is the only inteipretation-then we remove the minister's objection to the letter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me say a
word at this point. Taking the hon. gentleman's own interpretation of the word "political," I ask him if he thinks it is a proper thing for an officer of this government, where a difference of opinion is supposed to exist between this government and the British government in regard to a particular matter, to refer that matter to an official of the United States government and ask his adverse comment upon it. Let me cite a narallel case. At this very moment there is a difference of opinion in this country as to the attitude the British government is taking on the question of preference. An officer of the Department of Trade and Commerce here might just as Dr. Torrance did in the case the hon. member cites, and according to his own interpretation, take the view that political pressure is responsible for the position the British government is taking in this matter. Would the hon. member think it a proper procedure for an officer of the department, without the knowledge of his minister, to communicate with the Department of Trade and Commerce at Washington, and ask him his opinion as to how the matter should be dealt with? If an officer of the department saw fit to act in that way, I do not wonder chat the minister would not have confidence in him.

The Prime Minister has missed the point. He says: "Without the knowledge of his minister". His minister instructed Dr. Torrance to ascertain how the United State's department would be affected. He instructed him to write this letter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Instructed him to refer to political considerations?

No. The Prime Minister based his argument a moment ago on the fact that the minister was ignorant of all this. I am pointing out to him, just in answer to that point, that Dr. Torrance was instructed to write that letter.
Not that kind of letter.

This letter is a confidential letter. It does not refer in an offensive way to political influence. There is nothing of an offensive character in the language, even though one chose to take that view which I cannot see any ground for. Let us examine the letter again. After several paragraphs 
to which the minister takes no objection, dealing with the whole question of quarantine, Dr. Torrance states:
If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine it places the scientific advisers of the respective governments in a very anomalous position, and I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
Then he goes on:
Should political pressure force me to accept a shortened period of quarantine for imports from the British Isles I have been wondering what would be the attitude of your bureau in regard to the matter.
What pressure could there be other than political pressure? The pressure is the relations existing between Canada and Great Britain as affecting the removal of the embargo in Great Britain and the shortening of the quarantine period in Canada. The word "political" is very properly used there. Dr. Torrance says this: "I believe our quarantine period of thirty days should be maintained, but this pressure, owing to these negotiations, may force me to shorten that period". He does not say this, but this, of
10 p.m. course, is inferred in the object of the whole correspondence-"Should I be forced to reduce that period, what are you going to do to our cattle? Are you going to shut our cattle out or are you going to increase your period of quarantine?" It must be borne in mind that these negotiations between the department in Washington and our department in Canada had been going on for years. They had been running on harmoniously in regard to these matters and the question was a very serious one. Dr. Torrance, at the instructions of the minister, seeks to find out what the attitude of Dr. Mohler would be. To show that Dr. Mohler took no wrong impression out of this, we have already read to-night a letter from Dr. Mohler showing that no such idea entered his head. Then, we have his reply which I might read again-I do not suppose that is necessary-a perfectly courteous reply that has in it no suggestion of there being anything offensive in this letter.
I want to make this appeal to the Prime Minister: Supposing he grants that there was in the wording of this letter something other than the skill of an experienced diplomat, would that be an offence for which a servant of his standing should be summarily dismissed? I put this to the Prime Minister? He is in charge of External Affairs; supposing an under-secretary of External Affairs wrote a letter that was not couched in quite the terms that he approved and he later ascer-

tained this; supposing this was the first time and that there was no more than this, would he dismiss him? He would not; I know he would not. He might bring him in and question the propriety of the exact language or something of that kind but he would not dismiss him. He would not bring him into his office; put a pen into his hand and say: Sign that resignation or you go out of here dismissed and disgraced. That is our complaint in this matter. Dr. Torrance was not given any opportunity. He is a man of the highest standing, a man of reputation, a man who has served this country well, a man who stands at the top of his profession, a man whose integrity and honour are not impeached by any one in this country other than by the minister and these two or three-the minister would not tell us who they were-unnamed, unrevealed scandalmongers whose statement was read to this House, and even the man who read it was ashamed to take responsibility for it. In addition to that, I have in my hand a sworn statement from Dr. Torrance that I intend to put on Hansard dealing with this whole matter. There should be no necessity for a sworn statement from him and no one in this House should ask for it; but when one is charged with innuendo and invidious allegations are made such as were read in this House the other day, and when such treatment is accorded under the excuse of this letter, it appears to be necessary to get the strongest possible evidence to support our contention. This is the affiadavit that Dr. Torrance has signed in connection with the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the
hon. member reads the affidavit, as I listened to the discussion since I came into the House this evening it was perfectly clear to me that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) did not desire at all to leave the impression that he was in any way reflecting on Dr. Torrance's character. He has made it clear that there was a lack of confidence between himself and Dr. Torrance. The particular act that he has referred to was an act which he felt, having regard to their existing relationship made it desirable that it should be terminated as soon as possible. But as regards the communication to which my hon. friend has taken strong exception, the Minister of Agriculture said this evening that he did not mean the words in the sense in which they are being interpreted at the present time by hon. members opposite, and I might say further that I think the minister is the last one who would in any way be harsh with an official of his department. He was ready to endeavour to meet Dr. Torrance's
wish in the matter of superannuation and the like. If in any particular that wish has not been met, to the extent to which it is possible to have it met upon report of the Civil Service Commission, made in accordance with the laws of the country, it will be the wish of the government to see that in that regard every justice is done to Dr. Torrance.

I am glad the Prime
Minister has made that statement; but he was not in his seat the other day when this previous discussion took place. Had he been in his seat, he would have understood what aspersions were heaped upon Dr. Torrance. The minister certainly to-night, faced outside of the House and in the House with a situation that was untenable for him, comes and places his whole stand on this letter of which I think the most harsh interpretation would not justify the action that was taken.
Let me read this affidavit by Dr. Torrance and let me call to witness the statement of the Prime Minister and the statement of the minister himself that he cannot find grounds for disputing the honour and the integrity of Dr. Torrance.
Statement of the circumstances leading to the retirement of F. Torrance from the position of Veterinary Director General.
On Saturday morning, July 7, 1923, I was in my office as usual when I received a telephone message to come over to the minister's office as he wished to see me. I went at once and found Hon. Mr. Motherwell alone in his office.
He asked me to sit down and said:	"I think the
time has come, Doctor, when we should part." He went on to say that he had lost confidence in me and when pressed for a reason, said that information from my office had reached the opposition. I vigorously denied having given any information other than any one had a right to have and said that if such information had reached the opposition it was not with my knowledge or consent.
He then said that he had a copy of a letter I had written to Washington which gave him ample grounds for my dismissal. Without letting me see the letter, he read a passage from it which he interpreted to cast a reflection upon himself and the government as likely to force me to take a course for political reasons which I did not approve. I explained that the reference was not to Canadian but to British authorities and reminded him that the letter in question had been written a long time ago, namely, last October, yet he had never objected to it until to-day. He would not accept any explanation.
He demanded my resignation and said'that unless it was forthcoming at once he was prepared to dismiss me. I said that this appeared to be a very harsh way of dealing with an official of my standing and service and requested to be given an opportunity of consulting my friends. He refused.
I then asked permission to see the Prime Minister. He said that the Hon. Mr. King was out of the city and in any case it would be useless to see him as my retirement had been considered by the government and decided upon.
He went on to say that if I resigned I would be entitled to retirement allowance under the Calder Act based upon seventeen years' service and, consulting a memorandum in regard to this, said-
Supply-Agriculture

The minister said.
I would receive about $1,400 or $1,500 a year. If I refused I would be dismissed without any retirement allowance whatever. He offered me paper-
I want the Prime Minister to hear this affidavit.
He offered me paper and pen and insisted that my decision be made instantly.
I then asked that if I resigned I might be given the customary six months' leave with pay. He replied that they desired to fill the position immediately, and if leave were granted they could not fill the position until the leave had expired. I suggested as an alternative a gratuity of six months' salary. He agreed to this.
I then asked if my retirement could not be postponed for a year when I would be sixty-five and ^ould retire on account of age. This was refused.
I felt it was useless to go further. I had to choose between two alternatives, either to fight an unjust dismissal with the whole force of the government arrayed against me or else to accept the terms offered and write out my resignation. I had no chance to consult any one and no time to think it over. I decided to resign, wrote out my resignation and gave it to him, at the same time making a copy for myself. Our interview then terminated.
I am told my resignation was before the council and accepted the same day.
I afterwards saw the Hon. Mr. King at his country residence but could obtain no redress. He however approved the granting of six months' leave. In the final adjustment this was changed to four months' leave and two months' salary as a gratuity.
My retirement allowance has not been arranged as agreed upon. My term of service has been cut down from seventeen years to eleven years and four months and my annuity from approximately fourteen hundred to nine hundred dollars.
This is a grave injustice. I was induced to resign by a definite statement that I was entitled to an allowance based on seventeen years' service and this arrangement has not been honourably carried out.
My services to the country have deserved better treatment. I was the responsible official when in 1914 the worst outbreak of foot and mouth disease in the history of the United States broke out in that country. It never gained entrance to Canada, not through good luck, but through the careful preventive measures adopted by my advice and carried out under my direction.
During my term of office cattle mange in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan was practically wiped out and the mange area abolished; dourine of horses was entirely eradicated; and losses from glanders and hog cholera reduced to a minimum. Active steps were taken towards the control of bovine tuberculosis. The meat inspection service was maintained at a high level of efficiency.
The Health of Animals branch of the Department of Agriculture gave further proof of its efficiency and value to Canada in connection with the removal of the British embargo on our cattle. The most valuable argument on our side was the freedom of our cattle from serious communicable diseases.
The branch over which I had the honour to preside for many years is largely responsible vor this happy state of affairs, yet its chief officer, responsible under the minister and his deputy for its policy and its efficiency, has received the treatment I have described.
F. Torrance.
Sworn to before me at Guelph, Ontario, this 31st day of March, 1924.
R. G. Johnson,


That is Dr. Torrance's statement, a fair
statement of fact. I draw the Prime Minister's attention once again to the statement incorporated in his resignation, acknowledged a day or two afterwards by the minister himself, indicating that an agreement or bargain had been made regarding Dr. Torrance's retiring allowance. Let me read the affidavit again in that regard:
He went on to say that if I resigned I would be entitled to retirement allowance under the Calder Act based upon seventeen years' service, and, consulting a memorandum in regard to this, said I would receive about $1,400 or $1,500 a year.
The minister prepared for this emergency, knowing exactly what he was going to dio. He had this memorandum under his hand when the consultation was taking place. Dr. Torrance had not the slightest notice of what was impending. He entered his office unsuspectingly and was met with a demand for his resignation. The minister had it all carefully prepared!. The other day he intimated that for six or eight months after knowledge of this letter he nursed in his heart this little grudge about "political considerations" and sought for corroborative evidence,-
Mr. MOTHERWELL; That is not so.

-which corroborative evidence he produced the other day-corroborative evidence of such a disreputable character that one would not condemn a yellow dog on it, leave alone a Civil servant-the disreputable character of which he has acknowledged and demonstrated in the fact that to-day he abandons it and seeks to avoid every reference to it.
Oh, 'oh.
It is awful.
Yes, it is awful. Hon. members laugh-
Don't get excited. You did worse .than that in 1911, you threw poor people on the street in a heartless and cowardly way. It was a cowardly act.

We quite agree with the hon member's designation of this act-it is certainly a .cowardly act. It is no laughing matter, nor is it a trivial matter, for a civil servant to be thrown out in this way. The least Dr. Torrance could have expected was to have been given an opportunity to defend himself, an opportunity to consult his friends, an opportunity to ponder the heinousness of the offence contained in that simple letter. But no such opportunity was granted him, no consideration whatever was accorded him.

Instead, by brutal strength, based upon unlimited power, his resignation was demanded or he would be forced on the street.

Mr. Chairman, what my hon. friend has said requires a little attention, and possibly I may have to repeat myself as a number of hon. members were not in their seats at the beginning. I have been accused of selecting the letters I read.
I stated to the committee at the outset that I would read as many letters as I thought would be of interest, and that if any further letters were required upon which some of those I intended to read were based I should be glad to read them, but that I did not want to clutter up Hansard any more than was necessary. But see what my hon. friend did in reading his extracts from Hansard. He got to a certain point twice, Mr. Chairman, and then balked solid. Let me quote:
Mr. Motherwell: It came through Dr. Mohler.
This is. the information, the report that he was surprised and so forth.
Mr. Meighen: Very well; but who said it?
Mr. Motherwell: I understand it came from Dr. Mohler.
Mr. Meighen: Did Mr. Mohler say that he was
astonished ?
Mr. Motherwell: Yes.
Why did he not go just a little bit further, one more step? I do not think he saw the next one; possibly he is colour blind or something like that. Now, what was the next one?	/
Mr. Meighen: Will the minister take the responsibility for saying that Dr. Mohler so stated?
Mr. Motherwell: I could not do that as he did not tell me.
"He did not tell me," showing, as I stated in the first instance, that the report had come to us that Dr. Mohler had expressed surprise that we kept a gentleman in our employ. That was the report that came to us, and when the right hon. leader of the opposition wanted to know if I would take the responsibility for saying that Dr. Mohler had said that, I replied that I could not, as he did not tell me. Yet my hon. friend, who pretends to be the quintessence of fairness to-day, balks like a balky horse just as he comes to that.

But the minister took
the responsibility for the statement that Dr. Mohler had told someone. It now turns out that Dr. Mohler told no one, and that the minister's statement was false.

I am very glad
to find that he did not. So much for that. I have not the place in Hansard where I 155
spoke the other night, but I am sure hon. members heard me two or three times state the reasons why I did not take this matter up with Dr. Torrance immediately after the letter came to my attention. There were two or three reasons why I did not do that. One was that I was busy preparing for the session, then the session was on. Furthermore I was desirous to give Dr. Torrance a second chance, which every man is entitled to, and to see if he would not cease his resentment. I understood1 the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to say that I admitted I nursed this resentment to Dr. Torrance and watched for an opportunity to trap him. I said the very opposite, that I gave him six months to retrieve himself, to live down his conduct.

Did the minister ever
speak to Dr. Torrance regarding this letter upon which he now bases his action?
I did not.
Not until July 7.

We will follow that up now. My hon. friends seem to be making much ado about very little. Dr Torrance is gone; I do not know that this will bring him back, but we want to do justice to him, we want to do justice to all. Now, so much for that. I gave him six months' grace, as I say, in which to do the right thing, but he did' not do it.

How did Dr. Torrance
know that he had done the wrong thing then?

I certainly told
him, as I have stated here about fifty times. Now, his resignation is here, as read by my hon. friend. How did the understanding regarding his retirement come about? I told Dr. Torrance distinctly that I could not tell, did not know, could not make a computation as to how much he was entitled to, but I said he would get all that was coming to him under the terms of the Calder Act. He said he was entitled to seventeen years, and I said, ''Well, whatever you are entitled to you will get." What did he think he was entitled to? I do not think the Prime Minister was here when we took that up. What did he say he was entitled to? This is what he told me:	He said he was entitled to
seventeen years, with the exception of some technicality with regard to the first six. I took him at his word. Of course I did not know whether that was correct; I had not seen the Calder Act at that time. I could

not compute it even now or say what it would come to at seventeen years. Based on his own figuring, it was SI ,500, and I said, "If that is what it is shown to me by the Calder Act, that is what you will get." It could not be otherwise. I did not know until some time afterwards what it would come to; in fact, I was astonished at the liberality of the allowance. As I said before, I could be accused of being too liberal, of computing his annuity in respect to two years in which he did not work one hour for the government. Yet I am accused of being unfair to him. Let us see how many hours he did work. I will go over that again as given in the letter of Mr. Jarvis, my assistant deputy minister, to the Civil Service Commission, previously referred to. Does the ex-minister assume responsibility for what the late government did in my county as far as cattle are concerned?

There was some delay in that connection, and the next thing following upon the passing of the legislation by the British government was the matter of agreeing upon the regulations. I quite agree that the deputy minister should have been one of the delegates to go over and arrange for these regulations. That is only natural, because he is a man of ability, a man whom everybody interested in agriculture in this country respects. However, when it comes to selecting a second man I believe a member of the Health of Animals Branch- Dr. Torrance, Dr. Hilton or some other capable man in that branch-should have accompanied Dr. Grisdale over there to assist in the formulating of the regulations, taking with them their expert knowledge of such matters, including the carrying out of the regulations, our regulations with the United .States, and other subjects that would crop up in the discussion. I would like to know if the minister considers it necessary to adopt more stringent regulations for the shipment of horses to British Columbia from Tia Juana, Mexico, than are necessary in the case of a shipment of horses from the same point to points in eastern Canada, and more severe and stringent regulations than are imposed against those horses shipped from the same points to other points east in the United States; and if so, -why?

My hon. friend's question is somewhat involved, but I think it means this: Are the regulations more stringent against horses coming from Tia Juana, Mexico, to western Canada than to eastern Canada? Is that it?
Yes.

Some horses were brought to eastern Canada before the regulations were put into force, .but the regulations are now the same all over Canada, east and west. I might say that the whole of British Columbia, especially the Department of Agriculture and the premier of the province, all the live stock associations, dairy associations, and fruit growers' associations, have been flooding me with telegrams asking me to keep out Mexican horses. They could not get to Canada without passing through that county in California, a desert, if you like, of thirty-five miles, that is infected with the foot-and-mouth disease. I was deluged also with telegrams from the race-track men and others interested in that sport in British Columbia to let these Mexican horses come through, and some of them were California horses; they asked us to violate our own regulations only a day or two after they had been laid down, in order to let these horses pass through that county in California infected with the foot-and-mouth disease. I could not do that.

With regard to the shipment of these horses, I would point out that the regulations are unnecessarily severe. I do not see why the minister should take the opinion of British Columbia fruit growers in preference to the opinion of his own veterinarians in that connection. I would have thought they were the people most familiar with the pathology of foot-and-mouth disease, and with what regulations were necessary to prevent it getting across into Canada. If the minister was not satisfied with their particular knowledge, he could have looked to the United States to see what they were doing. Surely the regulations adopted over there, [Mr. Tolmie.)
permitting the horses to be shipped east from Tia Juana are quite rigid and effective enough to prevent the entrance of the disease into those states, and would be just as good: to prevent the disease getting into British Columbia through the shipment of horses. I wish particularly to call attention to what the United States is doing in this regard. I have here a letter from Dr. Mohler, who is chief of the Bureau of Animal Industry, Washington, dated May 20, 1924, so it is only a day or two old:
Dear Mr. Tolmie,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of May 17 requesting information concerning the precautions that are being taken in connection with the shipment of race horses from Tia Juana, Mexico, through the State of California.
This season we have made arrangements to have our inspector who is stationed at San Diego, California, inspect these animals on the Mexican side of the border, and they are being loaded on the cars before crossing to this side. Such animals are permitted movement through non-infected sections of California without any restriction so far as this Bureau is concerned. In fact, our regulations, copies inclosed, issued in connection with the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease do not cover horses except that such animals cannot be moved from infected premises. A number of the States, however, will not admit any kind of livestock that originates in or passes through California. A few of the States that have very drastic regulations in this respect are Arizona, New Mexico and Texas.
Very truly yours,
J. R. Mohler,
Chief of Bureau Animal Industry.
That would indicate that in keeping out these horses from British Columbia the minister adopted even more severe regulations than were imposed by the Bureau of Animal Industry at Washington. These men in British Columbia, I understand, offered to ship these horses out through that comer of California that is not infected with the foot-and-mouth disease, over east to Omaha, up north to Moose Jaw, and then back over the mountains to British Columbia. As a stock owner and a stock breeder in British Columbia I would be one of the last to ask for any relaxing of the regulations that would endanger the health of animals in that *province. I might point out that in 1914-15, when you had 22 states infected across the line, and two or three right on the Canadian border, horses were allowed to enter Canada from the United States from non-infected areas, and not one single case of foot-and-mouth disease got across the line. These men in British Columbia have invested large sums of money in race tracks, and they were good enough to wire me to get the regulations for them from the Health of Animals Branch of the Department of Agriculture. I applied there, and I received information to the

A bad source.

I think it was a good source in this particular, and I think if my hon. friend had been in my shoes at the time his decision would have been identical with my own because there is this difference: I have the responsibility of doing everything that is humanly possible to keep out this foot and mouth disease. I have just received a number of photographs from California. I do not know whether they are ready yet or not but they present the most terrible pictures that I think I ever saw. There are great, long trenches, apparently much longer than these buildings, dug out to a depth of six or eight feet. The poor cattle are crowded in there just as thick as they can stand with men on either side shooting them down, then covering them up with lime, and steam shovels afterwards piling earth over them. There is one picture after another. Another series deals with hogs, and a third with sheep, all the animals showing signs of the disease with the saliva exuding from mouth and tongue. Now, to take the chance of admitting these horses from Mexico, and possibly permitting disease to enter with them, is something I could not take the responsibility for.

I quite agree that the
picture my hon. friend has drawn is a very horrible one, but why are regulations more necessary here than are required by the Bureau of Animal Industry in the states to the east? That is all I was asking for. I am not asking for any relaxation in the regulations at all. If I thought you were being asked to bring in horses from infected districts I would be just as strongly in favour of restrictions as my hon. friend. That is my point of view. I want to know why regulations are more necessary and more severe now than they were ten years ago, when we allowed horses to come in simply on inspection at the boundary line, a practice which was most successful and which did not result in the introduction of a single case of disease. The portion of California traversed by Tia Juana race-horses on their way east is not an infected area; there is no foot and mouth disease within a hundred miles. Seeing that American horses are freely shipped across this territory why not Canadian?

The answer to that is that they have got the disease and we have

If hon. gentlemen opposite are willing to sit here a little longer I am quite agreeable. I am sorry that such an important item as this will not receive the consideration it merits. We have been engaged in a political squabble to which no contribution has been made from hon. members in this comer. I congratulate my colleagues upon having the good sense to keep out of discussions of that kind.
With reference to Dr. Torrance my personal opinion is that he was a splendid man for the job. I am personally acquainted with him and I believe he was a very efficient officer. As regards his dismissal I have nothing to say. If he did not suit his superior officer perhaps that was sufficient to justify his being let go, but it should be allowed to remain at that. There is no use crying over spilled milk. I congratulate the minister upon the gentleman who has been appointed to take his place. In Dr. Hilton I believe we have one of the best men it is possible to procure. There is good reason why Dr. Hilton is such an efficient officer: He received his early training in the city of Portage la Prairie from which many good men have come. That is one reason I am glad Dr. Hilton has been appointed to this position.
I notice that the vote has been reduced this year by 8250,000. I want to ask the minister why the reduction has been made. This is a very important question among my people at home. There are certain regulations in regard to the accredited herd plan, and here I want to state that the inauguration of this system was one of the finest steps ever taken by any government. I desire to give full credit to the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) who was mainly responsible for the enactment of that legislation. There is a regulation I think that calls for ten pure breds before one can come under the application of the accredited herd plan. The department last year limited that to five but the fact is not generally known. Of course there is a reason for that. The government know that if the fact was widely understood they would simply be swamped with applications and they have not the money to take care of the expenditure that all such demands would involve. This is a very unfortunate situation and one that requires the careful attention of the government.
I also want to know if there are any applications in for restricted area work and if the government is in a position to take care of any
