applications that may come in in connection with that phase of the operations.

I have to thank my hon. friend for really getting at this late hour, and for the first time at the purpose of the vote. We have had to pay attention to hon. gentlemen opposite who have monopolized all the time, but I would not like the sitting to close without answering the questions my hon. friend has asked. The first question he asked was why the amount of the vote has been reduced. It only appears to be reduced as far as our activities are concerned, and the explanation is this: In the first place the vote had to take care of $150,000 or $250,000 of accounts of the year before. My hon. friend will remember in the supplementary estimates last year we brought down three-quarters of a million of dollars, and as a result of that we were able to pay up all the outstanding accounts that had been accumulating from year to year ever since I had the honour to take charge of the department. We are starting the new fiscal year with the accounts all cleaned up, and we will not have to spend $150,000 for that purpose. In addition to that we have seventy-five to one hundred thousand dollars more than is necessary-that is there is that much left over of what was voted. Consequently we can make a reduction of $250,000 in the total vote and still take care of fully just as much work as last year. The estimated number of additional herds is 1,500. We have now 2,800. We can do as much work with that vote as with the larger one for the reasons I have enumerated.
I think the next point was about having pure-bred herds of ten before we would deal with them under the accredited herd plan. The matter has been brought up twice during the last two years, and I think very properly. There are many arguments to support the proposition that the herds should be as small as possible. What is the use of letting a beginner run his herd up to a large number and then discover they are all polluted with tuberculosis? Better take them when they are small, and if any are lost through tuberculosis the loss will be smaller accordingly. Notwithstanding that obvious fact, we decided to take on herds of five instead of ten, and we are going to see how it works out. The number of reactors in the second test has been considerably less this year, and if they keep on decreasing in that way we believe the extra amount required for the larger number of herds will be more than offset by the smaller number of reactions in the second test. We have to-day, I understand, nearly a thousand accredited herds. That was very noticeable in Manitoba after
the restricted area was established in that province and everything cleaned up. The second test showed a little bit less than one per cent of reactions six months after the first test. As a matter of fact we are not concealing it, and if my hon. friend can find two neighbours out in his district or near it where one man has three pure-breds and another two pure-breds contiguous to each other we will test them, so long as it does not entail a lot more expense in travelling. You cannot take a smaller number than two. One animal is not a herd.
Then my hon. friend mentioned the question of the restricted area. In Manitoba we established a restricted area at the request of the Department of Agriculture of that province. That is the only one we have undertaken yet. We have two or three applications from the province of Quebec and one from Saskatchewan, I understand. When Mr. Evans the Deputy Minister of Agriculture came to us I told him we were not prepared to start out on the policy of restricted areas because we had not the money to do it. I was in hopes we would be able to work out some policy in connection with the provinces and the municipalities whereby the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal authorities could combine all their revenues for this purpose and clean up by means of restricted areas. But the provinces are all pretty hard up, and I am sure that the municipalities are in the same position, and I do not see any hope of getting asistance from this direction; but we wanted some information. We established one area and got the information as to the cost and the percentage of reactors on the first test and on the second test. This information has been most valuable to us, because while we have not established any more restricted areas, we are at the stage of introducing the restricted area round the cities where they' want a pure milk supply, in view of the municipal order that exists. We will take Saskatoon for example; under the old municipal order, those who supplied milk to Saskatoon had to have their cattle all tested or the milk had to be pasteurized. That scattered these herds all over creation, maybe a hundred miles away, and the result was, the intervening herds not being tested, it was impossible to keep down the infection. Then we found on adjacent farms cows jumping over the fence or fooling with each other through the fence. Instead of having that condition in future, we hope to lay down a restricted area and clean up the milk entirely, as we did in Manitoba, and avoid re-infection such as has occurred in the past. We

have not any established as yet. The people do not understand yet what it means. It may seem ridiculous to be spending all this money on account of the cattle and of the public health; but at the same time cities will take very little pains in most instances in regard to seeing that their milk supply has been pasteurized. I am glad that the minister has explained that the government is prepared to take up the extension of this work where five pure breds are required instead of ten. I knew in a casual way that that was the policy of the government, but I also knew that the people in general did not know it, but after this discussion to-night it will be generally known, and I think that many applications will be sent to the government resulting from this knowledge.
In regard to the restricted areas, while we do not want to butt in on anything going to Quebec, we have one of these areas in Manitoba, and I know that the people of my county are desirous of going into it. I believe that 75 per cent of the cattle are under the test, and it will be an easy matter to get the district surrounding Portage la Prairie to come into this area.
The minister makes reference to the provincial governments, and suggests that the municipalities might co-operate with the government in the work. That will have to come, if we are going to have efficient work done

such as they have in the United States, where compensation is paid only where the state government will pay part of the amount and the municipalities will contribute also. I believe we should all become interested in this work, if we are going to carry on an aggressive campaign.
I am sorry that I have to impose a few more remarks upon the committee, but if I know anything about anything I know something about this matter. I have stated before in this House that mine was the first application from western Canada in regard to the accredited herd plan. I had only one reactor, and in the course of time I got my certificate, and I have a story to tell in that regard, but I will deal with that later. Last year I mentioned to the minister that, in view of the fact that this government was spending millions of dollars to take care of the work, we should use every precaution against contamination. I suggested that where the Dominion government gives grants to fair boards they should insist that all cattle that come on the fair ground should be tested for tuberculosis. The minister thought it was a suggestion that was worthy of consideration. I felt inclined to bring a resolution into the House this year and have a debate on it and a vote of this House taken to see whether that should be the law of our land. Last fall I wrote to the secretaries of nearly all the large fairs in Canada, especially western Canada, to get their views on this important matter. They practically all wrote back telling me that this was a step in the right direction, but that they believed that we had not yet reached a stage where it would be wise to attempt legislation of that kind. I also wrote to the minister, and he will remember that he replied stating that he believed this was coming, but that the step was too radical at present. I also wrote to Dr. Mohler, chief of the Bureau of Animal Industry in the United States and asked him if they had any federal legislation similar to what I suggested. He replied that there was no federal legislation, but that many of the state fairs and some of the county fairs had already insisted and required that all cattle entering on their fair ground must be subjected to the test. I think some of the Canadian fair boards will take this matter up even ahead of the government if they do not step a little faster. I do not believe it will work much of a hardship if all cattle entering fair grounds must first be subjected to the test. In the restricted area in the Carman district they put on a fine agricultural show and all cattle exhibited must be tested; this was the case last year. Then we went on to Portage la Prairie where we did not

Speaking further relative to contamination at fairs, last year I remember reading where, in the Jersey islands, tuberculosis was unknown until two or three years ago. They traced the contamination directly to a herd of Jersey cattle that had been taken over and exhibited on the continent. This opened their eyes to the danger and now they will not allow any more of their cattle to be exhibited on the continent or in the British Isles. That proves that if you keep your herds free from infection by coming into contact with the disease, it is possible to keep your cattle pure for hundreds of years. I might give a personal illustration. I said that my certificate had been taken away from me last
12 m. year. The inspector came out to give me the annual test which the law calls for and one of my cattle reacted. She was a show cow, a cow that I had paid a thousand dollars for, and naturally I did not like to see her go down. They gave her the intradermal test and the ophthalmic test. They did not give her the subcutaneous test. They thought the two tests were sufficient, and the intradermal test was the only one to which she reacted. I followed her to Winnipeg;-we had her killed there, and we could find no lesions. I felt very sore over this, and if ever a man had occasion to be a little sceptical of this test, I had; but I had boosted for the accredited herd plan and I was game and took my loss. I think there should be some improvement in the law in this regard. This was a very valuable cow; she was a loss not only to me but to the whole Dominion. I said to the inspector: "What are you going to do about it?" He said: "I will have to ear-mark her; that is the only thing I can do." I said: "Call up Dr. Still and see what he will say about it." He said: "It will be no use, Harry; the law says 'once a reactor, always a reactor'; we will not be able to test her again." I said: "All right; go ahead and do your duty." In a case like this, we cannot afford to lose these cattle. Although she reacted, she did not have the disease, and in a case like this an owner should have the privilege of segregating a valuable animal and have the government retest it at the end of sixty days or ninety days, whatever the period might be. Then, 156
if she does not react, he should have the ' privilege of admitting her to the herd again There is room for some improvement along that line and I just make the suggestion.

I should like to
thank my hon. friend (Mr. Leader) for the suggestions he has made. We have never differed on this question since we met in this parliament, except on one point and that was the amount of indemnity and the advisability of reducing it. I think at this date my hon. friend will not disagree with me on the advisability at that time of reducing it and getting more value out of the money. I want to pay the hon. gentleman the tribute of saying that he has given us some valuable suggestions. Many of them we have carried out, and I think he should be satisfied with himself that he has made a real contribution to the improvement of this act and service.
With regard to exhibitions, I will just say a word. At all the exhibitions I visited recently I have found that the tested and untested cattle were kept quite separate, isolated, so that there would be no fear of contagion. In the Maritime provinces the tested cattle were in separate buildings altogether, so that we are doing all we can with regard to the question of contagion through the medium of exhibitions, consistently with not crippling the exhibitions. I do not think there is much contagion in that way now.

The minister has touched upon restricted area as carrying out the accredited herd system. I believe there are only a few places so far where that has been adopted. How does that affect, for instance, the breeding of beef cattle? People engaged in that business usually purchase them at the stockyards and ship them into the districts where they reside. Would that be permissible in a restricted area? What are the regulations with regard to the matter?

I do not know
whether my hon. friend just came in or not.
I heard the discussion.

I do not need to repeat what I said about the restricted areas with regard to the numbers. No cattle of any kind are allowed to enter restricted areas without themselves being tested, or otherwise you would reinfect the whole area.

Consequently the
benefit would aecure only to those engaged in dairying. This would really put a stop to the breeding of cattle for beef in those areas

It would be impossible to purchase on the market and ship in several carloads without having them subjected to the test.
Indiscriminate shipment without testing is not allowed, but beef cattle, like any other cattle, can be tested.
They would not be allowed into those areas without being tested?

No. The restricted area in Manitoba is very proud of its area. It thinks the cattle inside that area are worth a great deal more than those in any other part of Manitoba, other things being equal, because cf no infection being within that area. They are very careful to safeguard it and to avoid, in every possible way, reinfection.

The cattle would not be any more valuable than the others, once they were shipped out on the market as beef, and it would prevent people from purchasing on the market short-feed cattle, for feeding for three, four or six months.

They would not be more valuable as regards insurance because that is a flat rate by the packers, but if my hon. friend were buying beef, he would know that the risk of infection was reduced to the minimum.
So far as the reports have come in, do the people of that district seem perfectly satisfied with what is being done?

Yes, ll have had quite a time trying to hold them down from extending the area all over Manitoba. Adjoining municipalities have been very strong in their desire to be attached to this area, and my only regret is that we have not enough money to give them the opportunity. The area, however, was large enough to give us the information we sought; while a larger area would have meant more extended service, it would not have given us any more information.
Only part of that area is in my own constituency, and I have had but a limited opportunity of making personal inquiries from the men who were interested-; I found they were all satisfied.
Thank you.
If cattle are purchased in the stockyards for feeding in other restricted areas, are there facilities for testing them before they go out?
I understand they are tested, the facilities being such as are usually found around stockyards.
The one test is not sufficient.

It is sufficient to let them in, and they would- come in with the rest for the second test.
Mr .SUTHERLAND: And the -third?
I have a few other questions in connection with the Health of Animals branch. Will the minister grant me the privilege of asking these questions under the live stock vote?
Yes.

There is a phase of this question which may be connected somewhat with the department of health, but I think it can be handled more effectively under this department. I am quite in agreement with the value of the work of this department, particularly the accredited herd system for the eradication of tuberculosis, and I think the officers should be congratulated upon the advance they have made in cleaning up the pure-bred herds. This system was only started in 1919, and it was 1922 before we had any tubercular free herds under it. In that year we had eighty-sdx herds, and on March 31, 1924, we had 908 herds free of tuberculosis, at an average cost of $318 for compensation.
There is a ph-ase of this question which I believe is of very great importance, particularly as it deals with the health o-f our people. I refer to those -grade herds that supply m'ilk to our smaller urban centres. Some of these are tubercular free herds, but I believe 90 per cent of the milk f-rom such herds goes to the larger cities, where it is-pasteurized, and thereby rendered free from infection of tuberculosis. There was a time in the history of the country when some doubt was entertained as to the transmissibility of bovine tuberculosis to human beings, but today there is no question whatever in the minds of the best informed authorities in this and other countries as to the danger of infection, particularly of children, from milk derived fiom tubercular affected animals. In this connection I might quote from a bulletin on tuberculosis published by the Canadian Tuberculosis Association.
It is, however, in its communicability to children through milk bovine infection that the importance of bovine tuberculosis is most apparent. That this is a very real danger is proved by the careful statistics

of the percentage of the bovine type of tuberculosis in young children gathered by Park and others. The figures vary considerably in different localities.
This is taken from an address of that very much discussed gentleman, Dr. ' Torrance, when he was Veterinary Director General, delivered last year at the annual meeting of the association at Edmonton. He giv-es these figures:
Dr. A. Philip Mitchell, Resident Surgical Officer, Royal Hospital for Sick Children, has tabulated 72 cases of tuberculosis of children under twelve and found that 65 were of bovine type and only 7 of human type.
And) this is the analysis:
Children five to twelve years of age, human bacilli 4; bovine, 30. Children under five years of age, human bacilli, 3: bovine, 35. Grand total, 72 cases.
He says of this:
A most striking fact brought out is the high incidence of the disease in children under three years of age. This is not surprising when it is recalled that the large majority of children of this age are nourished in whole or in part on cows' milk. I find that in my series of cases, 84 per cent of the children have been fed with unsterilized cows' milk since birth.
There is another case which I think will come very readily to the minds of officials of the department. I refer to the city of Saskatoon, where some years ago the children's hospital was filled with children suffering from tuberculosis. After three years' protection by having cows inspected) under the municipal order plan, so that all the milk came from animals free from tuberculosis, the medical health officer of that city made the statement that their hospitals are free, not a child from the municipality of Saskatoon in those hospitals suffering from this disease; the only children there so suffering being those brought in from outside.

In view of the fact that possibly every tenth grave is premature because of tuberculosis and that a large percentage of these cases have been proven to be of bovine origin, this is a matter of the utmost importance to the public generally and particularly to those who are using unsterilized milk. I have here an item taken from a press report dated from Montreal, May 8, which says:
Deaths from tuberculosis in April in the city of Montreal represents 85 per cent of the total number of cases reported at the city hall, according to the statistics furnished Wednesday by Dr. S. Boucher, director of Public Health. Out of 153 cases registered, there were 131 deaths from this disease.
If in Montreal, as in other places, 85 per cent of the total deaths in a month were from tuberculosis, surely the disease constitutes a serious menace. Probably figures are never very intresting, but there has come to my attention from different sources instances which illustrate the great danger to the children of this country from this disease. During one of the official tests of my herd of pure-bred cattle the inspector related an instance of a couple of children near Brockville, Ontario, at a place he visited in the course of his work to test some cattle. When he arrived at the farm he found both children, a boy and a girl, suffering from tuberculosis of the bone, and crippled. He went on with his work, the cattle were tested, and to his surprise every cow in the herd was condemned. They were found not only to be reactors, but when the carcasses were examined there was not a carcass in the herd that was fit for food, showing a very exceptional prevalence of disease in that herd. The energy with which the work of eradication of bovine tuberculosis has been
Supply-Agriculture

carried on in this department is to a great extent the result of the interest taken in the matter by the late Dr. Rutherford. If I have the story correctly, his only son died from tuberculosis some years ago and the result was a firm determination on Dr. Rutherford's part to fight this disease wherever he found it.
I was informed of another incident in the town of Portage la Prairie. On this occasion the city was under the control of the health authorities who refused to allow any raw milk to be sold in the city except from tested cows. A man on the outskirts of the city had a family cow which upon being tested proved a reactor. The man was so annoyed at this and had so little faith in the tuberculin test that he said if he could not sell milk in the city he would use it for the purposes of his own family. Some time after this one of the children took sick and the doctor was called in, but the child eventually died. Subsequently another child, a little girl, took sick and showed the same symptoms, whereupon a suspicion was aroused in the mind of the doctor that there must be something wrong with the supply of milk. He asked the veterinary who had been making the tests if he knew anything about this cow, and was informed that the cow had reacted. The doctor went back to the father of the children and said to him, "There must be something wrong with this cow." The man scoffed at the idea for a while, but after brooding on the subject for some days he decided that the cow would have to be slaughtered and an examination made. The cow was slaughtered at the abattoir. The veterinary was in attendance, and to his surprise and horror he found that just above the udder of this cow there was a tubercular sac and that every movement of the cow caused the poisonous fluid, filled with germs of tuberculosis, to flow into the udder. Small wonder these two children were infected and ultimately died, and no wonder that that father was heartbroken over his lack of information and his failure to realize the grave danger to which his family had been exposed through the presence of this disease. I can cite a great many cases similar to this where from one cow several children have been proved to be infected with the disease. A case was mentioned at this same Live Stock Union meeting by Dr. Snyder of Montana. He said that down in Paris, Illinois, a breeder had his herd tested and among them was a vigorous, fine looking, fat animal that looked anything but tubercular. However, she reacted and was tagged. The breeder scoffed at the idea that that cow could be infected with tuberculosis, and he eventually removed the tag and turned her over to his hired man in lieu of wages. This .man had a family of five or six children, and IMr. Brethen.]
the eldest child, a girl, became infected with tuberculosis. Upon examination two of the other children were also found to be in different stages of this disease. Only two of them escaped, a baby six months old, and a little girl who had not touched the milk. People were horrified at the results to this family, and they wanted to have the man prosecuted at once, but the attorney general of the state said:	No, we will just let this stand for
the time being, and when this girl dies, as she surely will, we will bring action for manslaughter against the man who had sold this tubercular cow.
There are a great many cases where single individuals and whole families, particularly children, have become infected in this way through tuberculous cows, and when we realize the potential danger from a single infected cow we will recognize what it means to the health of the community generally when the Health of Animals branch has removed this danger, as a result of the accredited herd sj'stem, so far as tens of thousands of cows are concerned.
I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the situation that exists in our smaller towns and villages, where practically every pint of milk that is offered for sale is sold in its raw state. I believe that in 90 per cent of these cases no examination whatever is made as to the health of the cows. If we take the figures that this department has established in regard to pure-bred herds, which show from 14 to 18 per cent are found to be tubercular, we can easily recognize the potential menace that this milk is to hundreds of thousands of children in this country. The danger is not so great in the larger cities, where it is practically compulsory for the milk to be pasteurized. I believe Montreal is an exception. But in all the smaller places the milk is sold in its raw state, and there is nothing to prevent thousands of children being infected in their early days through drinking it. I believe this department should extend the operations of the accredited herd system so as to include herds of grade cattle that are supplying milk to these smaller towns. I do not know that you can make it compulsory, any more than you can in the case of the pure-bred herds, but wherever there is a milk dealer with ten or more cows furnishing milk under these circumstances, and he wants to go into the accredited herd system, I believe the money of this department, which after all is the money of the people of Canada, should be devoted to that purpose, to encourage the sale of pure and uncontaminated milk to the children of this country.

Knowing as I do what can be done with a little money in the eradication of this disease, I hold the members of this House responsible for the misery and sickness and death of thousands of children if they refuse to vote the money for this purpose.
We hear in these days a great deal about economy but what is true economy after all? We have sanatoriums established all over this country for people suffering from this disease, and if you put the cost of maintaining a patient in one of these institutions at the regular cost of three dollars per day, it only takes the cost of maintaining one patient for a few months to pay the whole cost of compensation for a herd of cattle. It is estimated that the value of a mature Canadian in his earning years is at least $6,000 a year, and when we consider that at least 9,000 people in one year went to premature graves in Canada because of this disease, you have there a wastage of $54,000,000. Where is the economy there? There are some diseases that money will not cure, but here is a very grave disease that expenditure of money can prevent. Only last year this department cleaned up over 500 herds by the expenditure of a little money, and in regard to these herds to which [ refer particularly, every pint of milk goes direct in its infected state to the children of this country. There is a very grave responsibility resting on every member of this House in this respect; I feel it resting on me or I would not have got up at this time of night to draw this matter to the attention of the committee. I believe the responsibility rests upon all of us here to make some effort to eradicate this source of danger to the children, the future citizens of Canada.
